newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Consolidation, short week.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Consolidation, short week.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are expected to take a breather and consolidate their gains at least for the first few days this week after topping the 7,000 millennium mark for the first time last Thursday.
Analysts say they would welcome any respite in the market after last week's gains to reduce the market's overbought condition and bring valuations down a bit.
Some said that with the recent losses in some high tech stocks, particularly among computer networkers, momentum players are finding themselves with fewer stocks to use as investment vehicles.
Trading will begin Tuesday after the conclusion of the three-day U.S. Presidents' Day weekend. The Dow closed down 33 points on Friday at 6989. It jumped 133 points in the week.

Grace Messner, vice president in charge of equity management at Wilmington Trust, said that with most of the major economic data for January out, there are no particular near-term catalysts to drive the market higher.

"It's hard to point to any event that will push us lower, but I think because we are so vulnerable at this level that there is plenty of room for a nasty surprise," she said. "Whether this will happen this week or next month, I have no idea. But the market looks like it is exhausting itself."
Anthony O'Bryan, technical analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons, said that a pullback to as low as 6850 on the Dow would do the market little harm and quite a bit of good at this point.

"A pause is not only normal but healthy because it removes price excesses and makes it easier to buy stocks," O'Bryan said. "You don't want to be buying stocks while they are hitting new highs. Even if they move just a point down you feel better about it."
The telecommunications sector could also get a boost from a pact made over the weekend to open the global telecommunications market.
The agreement, clinched by officials from 68 countries gathered in Geneva, puts the industry almost fully under the open trade rules of the World Trade Organization.

U.S. Trade Representative Designate Charlene Barshefsky said the pact would open new markets for U.S. firms, lower costs to consumers, and double or triple the size of the $600 billion a year telecommunications industry over the next decade.
A long list of U.S. telecommunications companies, including AT&T Corp, MCI Communications Corp and Sprint Corp, praised the deal.
Elsewhere, investors will continue to focus on the same groups which have been in the forefront of the stock market rally -- financial, drug and high technology stocks.
But not all high techs. The recent sharp losses in the networking sector have changed the environment for investment in technology issues, analysts said.

"We are seeing a separation between good techs and bad techs," O'Bryan said. Among "strong stocks" in the group, he named Intel Corp, Microsoft Corp, Dell Computer Corp and International Business Machines Corp, while listing others that are "stumbling," such as 3Com Corp and Cascade Communications Corp.
"This is still a strong area, but you have to forget about the stocks that have really been crushed," O'Bryan said. "Don't touch them. You can get hurt catching a falling knife."
The recent trouncing of several high-profile networkers has also scared momentum players out of the area, said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"The carnage in the information technology industry has linited the number of vehicles that momentum players can utilize," Metz said. "This has forced even more money into a smaller universe of blue chips, like the drugs and consumer staple demand stocks. The area has become overcrowded, stretched and quite vulnerable."
The market's performance would also depend heavily on the flow of cash into mutual funds, Roy Blumberg, chief investment strategist at Josephthal Lyon & Ross, said.

"That has been the driving force of the market over the past few months even more than the fundamentals," he said. "We are in an environment in which bad news is good news for the market and good news is good news for the market, too. It's a money thing that is happening right now."
Data this week include the January consumer price index on Tuesday and January housing starts on Thursday.
